seo_title: Stress Fracture Doctor in Jupiter, FL | Abacoa Podiatry
seo_desc: Foot stress fracture care in Jupiter and Palm Beach Gardens. Our podiatrists diagnose the crack, protect the bone and plan your return. (561) 915-1934
lede: A small crack in a foot bone can start as a dull ache on a run and become pain with each step. Our podiatrists help protect it as it heals.
what_it_is: A stress fracture is a tiny crack in a bone, or a deep bruise inside the bone, that builds up from repeated force rather than one big injury. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons notes that the metatarsals, the long bones that run through the middle of your foot to the toes, are hit most often, especially the second and third. The heel bone, the navicular on the top of the midfoot, the talus and the sesamoids under the big toe can crack this way too.

These fractures show up when activity climbs faster than bone can adapt. Runners, dancers, tennis and basketball players, military recruits and people who suddenly start walking much more are typical patients. Mayo Clinic notes higher risk in female athletes and in people with thinning bones, flat feet or rigid high arches. If you run or play around Jupiter and Palm Beach Gardens, a new race plan, a switch from the treadmill to outdoor running, or a busy season on the courts are worth mentioning to your podiatrist.
symptoms: Pain that builds gradually and gets worse with walking, running or standing
Pain that eases with rest, at least early on
A tender spot you can press with one finger over the bone
Swelling on the top of the foot or around the ankle
Pain that starts to linger at rest or at night as the crack worsens
causes: Increasing running or training miles, speed or frequency too quickly
Switching surfaces, such as from a treadmill to outdoor running or from a grass court to a hard court
Worn out or poorly supportive shoes
Weakened bones from osteoporosis, or low calcium and vitamin D
Foot shape, including flat feet or rigid high arches
Female athletes with low energy intake or irregular periods

how_therapy_helps.intro: Most foot stress fractures heal without surgery when the bone is protected from the load that cracked it. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons describes treatment built around rest, reduced weight bearing and protective footwear or a brace, with casting or surgery saved for certain locations and fractures that do not heal. The AAOS adds that fractures in areas with a poor blood supply, such as the base of the fifth metatarsal, heal more slowly, and Mayo Clinic notes surgery is more likely there. Our podiatrists match protection to the bone involved.
methods: Depending on the location, this can mean a stiff soled shoe, a walking boot or brace, or crutches for a period so the crack can knit, as both the AAOS and Mayo Clinic describe.

You stop the activity that caused the fracture and, when your doctor allows, keep your fitness with low impact options such as swimming or cycling, which the AAOS describes as good alternative activities.
A cast may be used when a fracture needs more stability than a boot provides, according to the AAOS.
Because low calcium and vitamin D and conditions like osteoporosis raise risk, your podiatrist may ask about diet, past fractures and bone health and coordinate with your primary care doctor.

The AAOS notes that some stress fractures need internal fixation with screws, pins or plates, most often in bones with a poor blood supply or fractures that do not heal with rest. Our doctors perform foot and ankle surgery when it is needed.
Once pain has settled and healing is confirmed, activity is added back gradually, with rest days in between, to lower the chance of a repeat fracture.

first_visit: At your first visit the podiatrist asks how the pain began, what changed in your training, your shoes and surfaces, and any history of fractures or thin bones. They press along each bone to find the exact tender spot, check swelling and look at your foot shape and gait. Because early stress fractures often do not show on X-rays, the doctor may order imaging such as X-rays or an MRI and will explain how to protect the foot meanwhile.
recovery: According to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, a stress fracture typically takes 6 to 8 weeks to heal. Fractures in bones with a poor blood supply, or ones that have been present for a long time, can take longer, and Mayo Clinic describes recovery in terms of weeks or months. How quickly you get back to running depends on the bone involved, how early the crack was caught and how carefully you rebuild. Going back too soon can turn a small crack into a larger one that is harder to heal, so the return is done in stages.
self_care: Stop running, jumping or other activity that brings on the pain until you have been examined
Rest and elevate the foot, and apply ice wrapped in a thin towel for about 15 minutes at a time
Wear a supportive, stiff soled shoe rather than going barefoot or wearing flip flops
Ask your doctor before relying on anti inflammatory pain relievers, since Mayo Clinic notes they may slow bone healing
see_a_doctor: Foot pain that keeps coming back with activity or does not ease with a few days of rest
Pain that continues while you are resting or wakes you at night
Swelling, bruising or a point of tenderness over a bone
Trouble putting weight on the foot
A sudden snap, deformity or severe pain after a fall or twist, which needs same day urgent care

faqs.q: Can you walk on a stress fracture in your foot?
faqs.a: Walking on a stress fracture keeps loading the cracked bone and can make the crack larger. Some fractures can be managed in a walking boot or stiff shoe, while others need crutches for a period. The right level of weight bearing depends on which bone is involved, so it is worth having the foot examined before you keep walking or training through the pain.

faqs.q: How do I know if my foot pain is a stress fracture?
faqs.a: A stress fracture usually causes pain that builds over days or weeks, worsens with activity and improves with rest, plus a small spot that hurts when you press directly on the bone. Swelling on the top of the foot is common. Other problems such as tendon irritation or ball of foot pain can feel similar, so an exam and sometimes imaging are needed to tell them apart.

faqs.q: Why didn't my stress fracture show up on an X-ray?
faqs.a: Mayo Clinic explains that stress fractures often cannot be seen on regular X-rays taken soon after the pain starts, and signs of healing may not appear for weeks. That is why doctors sometimes order an MRI, which Mayo Clinic describes as the best way to find a stress fracture, or a repeat X-ray later. A normal first X-ray does not rule one out.

faqs.q: What is the fastest way to heal a stress fracture in the foot?
faqs.a: There is no shortcut that lets a cracked bone skip healing time. The things that help most are protecting the bone early, stopping the activity that caused it, getting enough calcium and vitamin D, and following a gradual return plan. Catching the fracture early matters, since Mayo Clinic notes early treatment can speed recovery and lower the risk of complications.

faqs.q: Can I keep running with a metatarsal stress fracture?
faqs.a: Running on a metatarsal stress fracture is generally not advised. The repeated impact is what caused the crack, and continuing can lead to a full break or slower healing. Many runners keep their fitness with swimming or cycling while the bone heals, if their doctor agrees, then rebuild mileage slowly once the foot is pain free and healing is confirmed.

faqs.q: How can I prevent another stress fracture?
faqs.a: The AAOS and Mayo Clinic both suggest increasing training by no more than about 10 percent per week, mixing in low impact cross training, replacing worn shoes and keeping calcium and vitamin D intake adequate. Strength training helps too. If you have had more than one stress fracture, ask your doctor whether your bone health or foot mechanics should be checked.

signOrSymptom: foot pain that worsens with activity
swelling on the top of the foot
pain at rest or at night

notes_for_reviewer: Sources disagree on NSAIDs: AAOS OrthoInfo lists NSAIDs with RICE, while Mayo Clinic says NSAIDs may slow bone healing and suggests acetaminophen. The page follows the Mayo caution in self care. Please confirm your preference.
ICD-10 M84.37 is the non billable category 'Stress fracture, ankle, foot and toes' (verified on ICD10Data); billing requires the site, laterality and 7th character child code.
The practice does not list in-office imaging, so the page says the doctor 'may order' X-rays or MRI. Confirm wording.
Shockwave, MLS laser and PRP were intentionally not presented as stress fracture treatments, since the fetched sources do not support them for this condition.
The local line about running and court sports is a framing choice, not a sourced statistic, and no longer claims what the practice "often sees". Edit if it does not match your patient mix.
